hints: Notice the question contrasts area under versus gradient of displacement-time and velocity-time graphs.
Recall that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
Recall that gradient means $\Delta y / \Delta x$, so check which graph has change in velocity on the vertical axis and change in time on the horizontal axis.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: a displacement-time graph plots $s$ against $t$, while a velocity-time graph plots $v$ against $t$.
State the defining rule: acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$.
Link the rule to graphs: a gradient is $\Delta y / \Delta x$, so $\Delta v / \Delta t$ is the gradient when $v$ is on the y-axis and $t$ is on the x-axis.
Contrast the other cases: gradient of displacement-time gives $\Delta s / \Delta t = v$, and area under velocity-time gives $v \times t = s$.
Therefore acceleration is found from the gradient of a velocity-time graph. This is option D.

options.A: Area under a displacement-time graph multiplies displacement by time and does not give acceleration.
options.B: Area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement, $s = v \times t$, not acceleration.
options.C: Gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity, $v = \Delta s / \Delta t$, not acceleration.
options.D: Gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$.
